R08-C-01: Complaints that the news is too gloomy are as old as newspapers themselves, and they usually take the form of an accusation: editors, it is said, prefer misery because misery sells, and they feed their readers a steady diet of disaster in the knowledge that calm and contentment do not move copies. The accusation is not exactly false, but it misplaces the problem. Most of the skew in what reaches the public does not come from a taste for bad tidings. It comes from a definition of news itself, which privileges what is sudden, unusual and attributable to a single moment. A factory that closes on a Tuesday is news; a thousand small firms that open over a decade are not, because no single day contains their story. This definition has consequences that no individual editor intends. Events that are rare are reported precisely because they are rare, and the reporting makes them feel common. A reader who encounters three stories about aircraft accidents in a month may come away more afraid of flying than of driving, although for most travellers the ordinary hazards of the road, which seldom make headlines because they occur every day, are far greater. The same mechanism works on trends. Improvements tend to be gradual and diffuse, deteriorations are often abrupt, and so a society that is slowly getting better at something can easily believe, from its news, that it is getting worse. It would be a mistake to answer this by demanding more good news. Stories chosen because they are cheerful would be as unrepresentative as stories chosen because they are alarming, and readers sensibly distrust outlets that seem to be managing their mood. Nor can journalism simply abandon the unusual. A fire in a crowded building matters, and the fact that most buildings do not burn is no reason to stay silent about the one that did. A press that reported only what is typical would be not more accurate but merely less useful, since the typical is, almost by definition, what its readers already expect. Novelty is a legitimate test of what deserves attention; the error lies in letting it serve as the only test. The more promising remedy is to report the denominator alongside the numerator. A story about a crime can say whether such crimes are rising or falling; a story about a drug's side effect can say how many people take the drug without harm. A newsroom could also give slow developments a regular place, treating a ten-year change in literacy or infant survival as worthy of the front page even though nothing happened on the day it was printed. None of this asks reporters to cover less; it asks them to say more about the scale of what they cover. Such measures will not make the news a faithful miniature of the world, and they should not try to. Their aim is more modest: to ensure that what is exceptional is presented as exceptional, so that readers can tell the difference between what is striking and what is typical.
R08-C-02: For most of the twentieth century, readers of newspapers paid only a fraction of what their papers cost to produce. The rest came from advertisers, who were buying not journalism but attention, and the arrangement was so familiar that few people thought about it. Readers believed that they were buying a newspaper; in commercial terms, they were the product being sold. When advertising money migrated to online platforms that could target audiences more precisely, many news organisations turned to the readers themselves and asked them to subscribe. The change has been widely welcomed, and with some reason. A publication that lives on subscriptions answers to the people who read it rather than to the firms that want to sell them things, and it has less incentive to chase the cheap, fleeting clicks on which online advertising depends. Yet the subscription model carries a cost that its admirers tend to pass over. Advertising, whatever its faults, made news cheap for the reader and therefore widely shared. A wall that admits only paying readers divides the public into those who can afford careful reporting and those who cannot, or will not, pay for it. The second group does not stop reading. It turns to whatever is free, and what is free is increasingly material that is cheap to produce: opinion, aggregation, rumour and content funded by people with something to promote, whether a product, a cause or a candidate. The result is a two-tier system in which the quality of what one knows depends partly on what one spends. This matters more for news than for most products because the value of good reporting does not stay with the person who buys it. A voter who is misinformed about a local budget affects the outcome for neighbours who read every line of it, and a neighbourhood in which most residents rely on rumour about a planning dispute will reach worse decisions, which the careful reader who paid for accurate coverage must then live with. In this respect news behaves less like a private purchase and more like public health: the well-informed are not fully protected if those around them are not. The conclusion to draw is not that news should go back to an advertising model that has largely collapsed, nor that we should pretend that journalism can be given away without someone paying for it. Free news was never really free; its price was simply hidden in the cost of the soap and cars its advertisers sold. The question is how to keep the independence that reader revenue brings while limiting the exclusion it creates. Some answers are familiar: lifting the wall for stories of urgent public importance, cheaper access for students and libraries, and public or philanthropic support for reporting that markets will not fund. None is sufficient alone. But a news system should be judged not only by the quality of its best journalism but by how many people that journalism actually reaches.
R08-C-03: Among the habits that journalists learn early is the instinct to give both sides. When a council proposes a new road, the reporter calls the residents who want it and the residents who do not; when a minister defends a policy, the opposition is asked to respond. The habit is a good one wherever the disagreement is about values or interests, because there the reporter has no standing to declare a winner, and readers are entitled to hear the competing cases at comparable length. To do otherwise would be to editorialise under the cover of reporting, settling a political question by the simple device of quoting only one side. Difficulties arise when the same habit is carried over to questions of fact on which the evidence is heavily one-sided. Suppose that nearly all the researchers who study a question have reached one conclusion, and a handful dissent. A report that sets one scientist from each camp side by side, allotting them equal time, is scrupulously fair to the two individuals and seriously misleading about the state of knowledge. The reader, reasonably assuming that a newspaper does not stage contests between unequal parties, infers that the field is evenly split. Repeated over many reports, the impression hardens into a belief that the experts are hopelessly divided, and a reader may then feel free to choose whichever answer is more congenial. The format has communicated a falsehood that neither speaker uttered. The obvious objection is that journalists are poorly placed to judge which scientific views are sound, and that the history of science contains majorities that turned out to be wrong. Both points are true, and neither rescues the practice. The reporter is not being asked to decide who is right, only to describe accurately how opinion within a field is distributed, which is itself a matter of fact that can be checked. And the occasional vindication of a lone dissenter is not a reason to present every dissenter as half the story; most minority positions in science are minority positions because the evidence has gone against them. If a dissent later prevails, it will be because the evidence changed, and the reporting can change with it. What the critique of false balance requires, then, is not the exclusion of minority views but their placement. A dissenting researcher can be quoted, and quoted fairly, as a dissenter, with the reader told plainly how far that view departs from the field. What the reader should not be given is the impression, created by symmetry alone, that the dissenter speaks for half of those who know the subject. Nor does the critique apply where science is genuinely unsettled; there, presenting rival hypotheses side by side is exactly right. The skill it demands is harder than either reflexive balance or reflexive deference: it is the skill of knowing which kind of question one is reporting on.
R08-C-04: Newsrooms once knew remarkably little about their readers. An editor could see how many copies were sold, but not which articles were read, how far, or by whom; judgements about what the public wanted were made on instinct, on letters to the editor and on the preferences of the editor's own circle. Today a screen in the corner of the room can show, minute by minute, how many people are reading each story, and a headline can be tested in two versions on live audiences, the weaker one retired within the hour. Critics regard this as the moment journalism surrendered to the crowd. The charge deserves a more careful answer than either its proponents or its targets usually give. The first thing to say is that the numbers are not lies. A click records a real decision, made by a real person, to open one article rather than another. What it records, however, is narrower than it appears. It measures the pull of a headline at the instant of choice, not the worth of what follows, and still less whether the reader was better informed for having read it. A story that disappoints everyone who opens it can outperform one that rewards every reader, provided its headline promises more. When a newsroom treats these figures as a verdict on its journalism, it is reading a measure of curiosity as if it were a measure of value. Curiosity matters, and a story that nobody opens informs nobody, but it is only one of the things a newspaper exists to serve. The damage done by this misreading is gradual. No editor decides to abandon difficult subjects; it is only that, week after week, the stories that perform poorly on the screen are given less space, fewer reporters and less prominent positions, and the subjects they belong to slowly thin out. Each individual decision is defensible, since space is limited and something must give way, and that is precisely why the cumulative effect is so rarely noticed until it is well advanced. Coverage of committee hearings, foreign elections and the routine work of public agencies is especially vulnerable, not because readers have rejected it but because the measure in use was never designed to register its value. It would be naive to conclude that newsrooms should switch the screens off. The instincts the screens replaced were not neutral; they reflected the tastes of a narrow group of editors, who often mistook their own interests for the public's. Some organisations now try to measure better things, such as how long readers stay, whether they return and whether they subscribe. These are improvements, though each can be gamed in its turn. The deeper lesson is that no figure, however refined, can settle what a public needs to know. Metrics can tell editors what readers choose; deciding what deserves to be offered remains a judgement that cannot be handed to the instruments.
R08-C-05: An investigation that changes a law or ends a career is remembered for its result, and the result makes it look like a sound investment. The reporting behind it rarely looks that way while it is under way. A team may spend months requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures, only to discover at the end that the story cannot be stood up, or that it is smaller and duller than it seemed. No publication can know in advance which of its inquiries will succeed, so the cost of the one that does must also cover the many that quietly fail. Editors who have watched a promising inquiry collapse after half a year learn caution, and caution, in a publication under financial pressure, usually means fewer inquiries. This uncertainty would matter less if the rewards of success flowed back to the publication that paid for it. Mostly they do not. Once a finding is published, rivals can report it within hours, and the citizens who benefit from a cleaner tendering process or a safer bridge are seldom the readers who bought the paper that exposed the problem. In the language economists use, the work produces benefits that spill over to people who did not pay for them, and goods of that kind tend to be supplied in smaller quantities than a society, if it could choose collectively, would want. The most important of those benefits is also the least visible. Officials who know that their accounts might one day be examined behave differently from officials who are sure that they will not be. A local administration that expects a reporter to read its contracts has a reason to keep them clean, and the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it. The contractor who decides not to inflate an invoice, because a reporter once asked awkward questions about a neighbouring council, will never appear in any account of what journalism has achieved. Investigative journalism therefore works partly as a deterrent, and like other deterrents it is judged unfairly by its visible output; a quiet year may be evidence of its success rather than of its irrelevance. Admirers of the form sometimes overstate its virtues. Investigations can be mistaken, and a reporter convinced of wrongdoing may read ambiguous evidence in only one direction, with real costs for the people named. Nor is every exposure a public service; some are driven more by rivalry or an appetite for scandal than by any public interest. But the case for supporting such work does not depend on its infallibility. It depends on presence. Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous; a single celebrated exposure every decade, however brilliant, does less to discipline the powerful than a modest but permanent habit of looking. Those who fund journalism, whether readers, donors or the public purse, should therefore value a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop.
R08-C-06: When a news organisation discovers that it has published something false, the conventional remedy is a correction: a short notice, often printed some days later and some pages away from the original, stating that the earlier report was wrong. Few people defend the correction as adequate, but the usual complaint, that corrections are too small and too late, misses the more interesting difficulty. Even a correction that is prominent and prompt may fail, and it may fail because of what a retraction asks the mind to do. The problem, in other words, is psychological before it is editorial, and editorial remedies that ignore this are likely to disappoint. Consider a report that a fire in a warehouse was caused by paint and chemicals stored carelessly in a back room. A day later the paper announces that no such materials were present. The reader is now asked to give up the only explanation offered for the fire and to put nothing in its place. Minds do not handle this well. People tend to understand events as chains of cause and effect, and a chain with a link removed does not simply grow shorter; it breaks. An account with a missing link is uncomfortable, and when asked later why the warehouse burned, many readers reach for the explanation they were told to discard, not because they disbelieve the correction but because the correction left them with no story at all. The false claim survives because it was doing work that the retraction did not take over. If this is right, the remedy lies less in the size of the correction than in its content. A retraction that supplies an alternative account, stating what did cause the fire, or at least what the investigators now think likely, gives the reader somewhere to go. Where no alternative is yet known, the correction can at least explain why the original claim was made and why it seemed plausible, so that the discarded belief is accounted for rather than merely forbidden. There is a familiar worry that repeating a false claim, even in order to deny it, will make it more familiar and so more believable. The worry is reasonable, but it should not lead editors to issue vague notices that never say what was wrong; a denial that does not name its target cannot replace anything. None of this makes corrections easy, and it does not excuse the haste that produces most errors in the first place. A newsroom that publishes a confident causal story before the facts are in has created a problem that no notice can fully undo, since the first explanation a reader meets enjoys an advantage that later ones must work to overcome. Readers who met the false cause first will often have repeated it to others, built further conclusions upon it, and forgotten where they heard it. The lesson for reporters is therefore double: be slower to supply a cause, and, when one has been supplied wrongly, be quicker to supply a better one.
R08-C-07: Few words in journalism are now used with as much suspicion as objectivity. To its critics it names a pose: the pretence that reporters, alone among human beings, can step outside their own experience and describe the world from nowhere in particular. Put that way, the ideal is plainly impossible, and the critics are right to reject it. But it is worth asking whether that is the ideal anyone ever seriously defended. In at least one influential strand of its history, objectivity was proposed not as a description of the journalist but as a remedy for the journalist's limitations. Precisely because reporters could not be trusted to be neutral, the argument ran, they needed a method that would restrain what their partiality could do to the record. The method in question resembled, in a modest way, the procedures of empirical inquiry. A claim was to be checked against more than one source; documents were to be preferred to recollection; and the reporter was to say where each piece of information came from, so that a reader or a rival could test it. On this understanding the objectivity belonged to the procedure, not to the person, much as a laboratory's results are trusted not because its scientists lack ambitions but because their work is arranged so that others can repeat it. A reporter with strong opinions could practise the method; indeed, the method existed for such reporters, since a reporter without opinions, if one could be found, would hardly need it. What happened over the following decades was a quiet substitution. The discipline of verification, which is laborious and often invisible to the reader, was gradually overshadowed by a set of outward signs that were easier to display: a flat tone, a reluctance to draw conclusions, the habit of pairing every assertion with a counter-assertion. These signs were meant to signal fairness, but they could be produced without any verification at all. A story could quote two officials making incompatible claims, check neither, and still look objective. The appearance had detached itself from the practice it was supposed to indicate, and in some cases it obstructed that practice, since a reporter who had established that one of the officials was wrong was discouraged from saying so. Much of the current attack on objectivity is in fact an attack on this degraded form, and to that extent it is justified. Where it goes wrong is in the alternative it sometimes proposes. If the remedy for false neutrality is for journalists to report openly from their convictions, readers are left to choose among the convictions of different reporters with no common procedure by which to test any of them. The proposal also concedes too much to the degraded form, accepting that objectivity simply is the flat tone and the paired quotation, and then discarding the whole inheritance on that basis. Candour about one's commitments is a virtue, but it is not a substitute for evidence; a frank partisan who has not checked the facts is no more reliable than a disguised one. It should be conceded that method does not solve everything. Verification governs how a story is reported, not which stories are chosen, and the choice of what to investigate remains shaped by the interests and blind spots of those who make it. No procedure can remove that influence, and a newsroom that believes its method has made it neutral will be blind to it. Yet the concession limits the claim rather than defeating it. The case for objectivity understood as method is not that it makes journalism impartial but that it makes journalism answerable: it allows a reader who suspects a report to find out where it came from and whether it holds.
R08-C-08: A familiar lament holds that the public has broken into pieces. Where citizens once read the same few newspapers and watched the same evening bulletin, they now inhabit separate streams of information, each tuned to its audience's prior beliefs, and the common ground on which democratic argument depends is said to have eroded. The complaint is heard from commentators of every persuasion, each of whom tends to blame the media favoured by the other side. The lament contains a real worry, but it rests on a picture of the past that deserves scrutiny, and the remedies it suggests follow from the picture rather than from the worry. The ideal of a single forum in which a whole society reasons together has an attractive genealogy. Its admirers point to the coffeehouses, reading societies and pamphlet wars of early modern Europe, where private individuals gathered to discuss public affairs as equals. Yet the gatherings so admired were open in principle and narrow in practice, confined largely to those with the leisure, literacy and standing to take part. The mass audiences of the broadcast era were broader, but their breadth was purchased by a different narrowing: millions listened, while very few were permitted to speak, and the range of views considered respectable was set by a small number of editors and producers. What looks in retrospect like common ground was in part a common silence about matters that the gatekeepers did not think worth raising. None of this means the old arrangement had no merit. A shared stock of reported facts, however selectively assembled, gave opponents something definite to disagree about. Two people who had heard the same bulletin could argue over what to do about a strike or a drought without first arguing over whether it had happened. That is the genuine loss the lament points to, and it should not be dismissed. But it is worth being precise about what was lost. It was not chiefly that everyone attended to the same things, which was never a requirement of self-government and was always enforced partly by exclusion. It was that disputes about fact could be settled, or at least narrowed, by appeal to procedures and sources that people on both sides accepted. Seen this way, the fragmentation of audiences matters less than the fragmentation of standards. Many publics can coexist in a healthy democracy, each attending to its own concerns, provided that when they collide they can appeal to shared ways of establishing what is true. A society in which different groups read different things but accept the same rules of evidence is plural, not broken. A society whose groups no longer recognise any common method for testing claims is in difficulty even if they all watch the same programme. The second condition is the more dangerous because it is harder to see: a shared screen can conceal the fact that its viewers no longer agree on what would count as showing that something is so. The distinction has practical consequences. Nostalgia for the mass audience tends to recommend the impossible, the restoration of a few dominant outlets with the authority to define reality for everyone, and it risks restoring the exclusions along with the authority. The more plausible task is to build connections between publics rather than to merge them: institutions trusted across divides to verify claims, and habits of reporting that show their evidence so that readers who distrust the reporter can still examine the work. Such arrangements are less comforting than the image of a nation gathered around one screen, but they ask for something a plural society can actually provide. Nor need the connections be grand. A local paper that publishes the documents behind its reporting on a disputed planning decision, so that both sides can read them, does a small part of the work that the lament imagines only a national institution could do.
